study.title: Functional magnetic resonance imaging providing the brain effect mechanism of acupuncture and moxibustion treatment for depression
study.study_design: Narrative review of fMRI studies on acupuncture and moxibustion treatment for depression
study.population: Review covers studies of patients with depression as well as healthy volunteers across referenced primary studies
study.disease_condition: Depression; also covers anxiety, irritable bowel syndrome, stroke, Parkinson's disease, heroin addiction, spastic cerebral palsy, carpal tunnel syndrome, post-traumatic stress disorder, functional dyspepsia, aphasia, epilepsy, Wilson's disease, and primary insomnia as referenced conditions

extraction_notes.note: This is a narrative review paper, not a primary empirical study. It does not report original participant-level data, specific sample sizes for most referenced studies, coordinates from neuroimaging tables, or detailed statistical values. All neural results are extracted from narrative summaries of cited primary studies.

No study arms, conditions, or participant-level data are defined in this paper itself. The arms/conditions/interventions extracted reflect general categories of procedures described across referenced primary studies.
No neuroimaging coordinate tables are provided in this review paper. All neural results are narrative summaries of findings from cited primary studies. Coordinates cannot be extracted.
Deqi/sensation data are not quantitatively reported. The review only notes that 'getting Qi' is a subjective feeling with no objective standard, as a stated limitation.
Blinding, expectancy, and credibility measures are not reported or assessed in this review paper.
Adverse events are not reported in this review paper.
No trial registration is reported. Ethics approval is not mentioned.

The paper describes brain effects and neuroimaging results from multiple different primary studies using different patient populations, acupuncture modalities, and methodologies without always clearly distinguishing which result belongs to which study. Results have been attributed to cited references where possible.

In the intervention descriptions, the review mentions acupoints across multiple different primary studies and contexts. It is not always clear which acupoints were used in which specific clinical study.
The coordinate space (MNI, Talairach) for any neuroimaging findings referenced is not stated anywhere in this review paper.

Figure 4 in the paper shows quantitative MRI data related to Wilson's disease (magnetic susceptibility mapping), not directly related to acupuncture treatment of depression. This appears to be included as a general neuroimaging methodology illustration. It is referenced in the paper's text in section 2.5 but is not directly an acupuncture result.
Specific sample sizes for the cited primary studies are rarely mentioned in the review text and were not systematically reported.

All extracted neural results are based on narrative summaries in the review text and represent the review authors' interpretations of the cited primary studies. Direct verification against primary sources would be required for meta-analysis.

The paper describes sham acupuncture methods only in general terms across multiple cited studies (Streitberger needle, VonFrey ciliary stimulation, brush stimulation, non-meridian sham points). Specific sham penetration details, location coordinates, and credibility procedures are not provided for any individual referenced study.
The review references '18 acupoints along nine meridians' in section 2.4.1 but does not list these individually or provide their associated brain activation patterns beyond a general narrative.
